transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2028-03-14 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~62 minutes
Attendees: Jordan (Redwood AE), Priya (Redwood SE), Liam (Product), Nora (CTO, Catalyst), Hassan (ML Lead), Amira (Sec), Ethan (Platform)

Auto-summary (auto-generated): Walkthrough of model catalog filtering, bench strategy and routing policies. Live Q&A on security and dedicated vs hosted economics. Next: pricing and bench kickoff.

[00:00] Jordan: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Jordan Keller, AE on the Redwood team. We've got Priya our SE and Liam product on the call. How's everyone doing?
[00:05] Nora: Good, thanks. Excited to see the catalog flow. We've been doing a bunch of internal scouting.
[00:09] Jordan: Great. Quick agenda: we'll show the model catalog in the Console, talk through our heuristics for choosing open models, show a compatibility matrix especially around quantization and kernel mapping, then Priya will demo a short bench harness and discuss routing/fallbacks. We'll leave 15 min for Q&A. Sound good?
[00:22] Hassan: Yep. Our main goals - we want to reduce cost per 1k tokens while staying under 200ms P95 for chat-ish workloads, and maintain a secure posture for PII. Timeline is 6-8 weeks to pilot.
[00:33] Priya: That's helpful context. When you say chat-ish, is it mostly short prompts (<=512 tokens) or longer threads (3-4k context)?
[00:40] Hassan: Mix. 70% short, 30% threads up to 8k. We're particularly concerned about cold-start latency on dedicated pools.
[00:49] Priya: Ok makes sense. We'll show how batching and prefix/KV caching help the mixed mix.
[00:55] Liam: I'll jump in with catalog heuristics first — we tag models by architecture family, quantizability, and observed kernel perf. The compatibility matrix maps model to recommended kernel and quant profile.
[01:05] [Liam shares screen - Console - Model Catalog]
[01:16] Liam: On the left you can filter by task, size, and hardware. For Catalyst I'd recommend starting with these open families — Llama-2 variants we vetted, some of the Mistral variants, and a few Falcon forks that quantize well on A100 and RTX racks.
[01:31] Nora: When you say "we vetted" — do you have bench numbers for the 8k chunking scenario?
[01:36] Priya: We do. In the bench sheet we'll run— we set up microbenchmarks for 512 and 8k contexts. For 8k, throughput obviously drops but kernel mapping and KV cache cut steady-state P95 by about 20-30% compared to naive runs.
[01:52] Hassan: Can you explain the KV cache behavior? If an inference node fails, do you lose KV cache and spike latency?
[01:58] Priya: Good question. So our runtime maintains per-shard KV caches in memory; when a node fails we do two things: we reroute to a warm standby (if Dedicated) or to a compatible variant in another region (hosted). There is a short reconvergence window where cold-fetching the KV for long contexts will add latency — typically a few 100ms to seconds depending on sequence length. We also support prefix caching at the request layer so for common system prompts you don't rebuild the entire KV.
[02:28] Amira: For our security team we need to know: is the KV ever persisted to disk or to external object stores? We have a policy against unencrypted persistence for PII.
[02:36] Priya: By default KV is in-memory and not persisted. For Private deployments we can support HSM-backed snapshots if you want an operator-managed archive for debugging, but that would be under your control and encrypted with your KMS. Hosted customers can opt into encrypted snapshotting but it's off by default.
[02:54] Ethan: Are there region residency controls? We have EU/RoW separation requirements.
[02:58] Jordan: Yes — routing policies can pin requests by tenant to regions. We'll show the policy UI in a bit. Also Dedicated and Private let you choose physical locales.
[03:09] [03:09] Liam: Back to the catalog. Here's a compatibility row for Mistral-7B — recommended kernel = fused-attn-v2, quantization = 4-bit Q5_K. We also surface an expected latency column derived from our lab runs on rtx-6000 style hardware.
[03:27] Hassan: Those rtx numbers — our infra is in-house on 80xx ampere-ish GPUs, not exact match. How should we interpret the latency column?
[03:34] Liam: The cell shows a baseline; we also provide a kernel mapping note that says "if you are on older Ampere, prefer the int8-kernel fallback and expect +10-20% latency." We include confidence bands and the exact bench commit id so you can reproduce.
[03:49] Nora: Can you point to the bench artifacts?
[03:52] Priya: Sure — here's the bench workbook link (short link): drive.redwood/demo/catalyst-bench-20280314. It includes the harness, the prompt sets (anonymized), and the bench runner that hits our benchmarking endpoint.
[04:05] Hassan: Nice. On pricing — we'll need a sense of cost delta between hosted vs dedicated given 2M tokens/day.
[04:12] Jordan: We'll send a cost matrix. As a rule of thumb, for sustained 2M tokens/day Dedicated will be materially cheaper after you commit to a pool. Hosted is easier to start but unit token price is higher. We'll include an amortized GPU cost view in the matrix.
[04:26] [04:26] Priya: Now I'll demo a short bench run — I'm going to run 100 requests at 512 tokens against a Llama-2 curated variant and then switch to an 8k context run. Expect some noisy artifacts in the live run.
[04:39] [screen share - bench runner - terminal output]
[04:45] Priya: Kickoff: 100x 512 test. Starting...
[04:51] [04:51] Terminal: request 1 ok, req 2 ok... p95 ~ 155ms
[05:03] Priya: So 512 tokens on this config with batching set to 8 we see P95 ~150-180ms, depending on tail. Switching to 8k context now — this will exercise KV and memory pressure.
[05:16] [05:16] Terminal: starting 20x 8k runs... some cold starts... p95 spikes 1.2s then stabilizes ~420-480ms
[05:29] Hassan: That cold spike is the concern. How does autoscale help? If there's a sustained increase in traffic, will the pool warm up and reduce those spikes?
[05:36] Priya: With Dedicated you can configure pre-warmed slots and keep alive policies; autoscale policies scale capacity ahead of load if you provide a prediction window. There's also a fast-fallback policy — if a node is overloaded we'll route to a quantized variant with lower cost but slightly lower quality, configurable per route.
[05:53] Nora: That fallback behavior — can we A/B test quality impact? We need a measurable QA signal.
[05:59] Liam: Yes — Redwood Optimize integrates evals and you can attach prompt sets to routes. We'll run scoring (ROUGE/BLEU/embedding-similarity) on responses and surface regression alerts. You can set thresholds to disable auto-fallback if quality drops below a threshold.
[06:16] Amira: On compliance: we need audit logs for every request and key rotation policy for KMS. What does Redwood expose?
[06:22] Priya: We emit request-level audit logs (redacted token content by default) with timestamps, model version, node id and route. For Private deployments you get full raw logs if you opt in, and KMS integration supports rotation and HSM-backed keys for enterprise. We also produce SOC2 artifacts and a compliance whitepaper.
[06:39] Amira: Will you share the diagram that shows where those logs live and how they're encrypted?
[06:44] Jordan: Yes we'll attach a redacted architecture diagram in the follow-up.
[06:49] [06:49] Hassan: Quick technical: how do you implement "compatible variant" routing? If primary is Llama-2 13B HF, fallback to a quantized 13B or to a smaller 7B?
[06:57] Priya: The routing policy allows you to list fallback tiers: same model quantized, same family smaller model, or cross-family with mapping rules. We also have pre-computed quality deltas in the catalog so you can see expected regression. The runtime will prefer variants that match tokenizer/arch to avoid tokenization drift.
[07:13] Ethan: Do you have tools to run a deterministic head-to-head on our hardware? We'll want to bring a node into our lab.
[07:19] Priya: Yes — we provide the bench harness (python) and you can run it in your lab hitting Redwood's bench endpoint or run it fully offline with our runtime container in Private. For on-prem we also have a small validation script that verifies kernel availability and then runs microbenchmarks.
[07:36] Nora: On model licensing — do you ship any models or is it pointers to HF / open checkpoints?
[07:41] Liam: For open models we reference canonical checkpoints and sometimes host cached artifacts for performance. We keep track of licenses and note any restrictions in the model detail pane. For enterprise we can discuss hosting copies under agreement.
[07:54] Hassan: Is there a way to pin a model version per-route and still get autoscaler updates? We want stable outputs for compliance.
[07:59] Jordan: Absolutely. Route-level model pinning plus rollouts is supported. You can pin to a commit/tag and do canary rollouts to a subset of traffic. Rollback is one click in the Console and you can configure automatic rollback on regression signals.
[08:18] [08:18] Amira: Who in Redwood handles security questions for the contract? We'll need a security review and probably an on-site audit.
[08:24] Jordan: Our security contact is Mara Bennett — I'll intro you in an email. We have an enterprise pack that includes audit support and a security questionnaire fill.
[08:33] [08:33] Priya: Back to bench specifics — if you care most about P95 tail, we recommend targeting a mix of warm slots and smaller batch sizes for chat to reduce tail latency. For throughput-oriented workloads batching larger helps. The Optimize tab will give suggestions based on the bench signal.
[08:53] Hassan: Can Optimize propose quantization profiles automatically?
[08:56] Liam: Yes. Optimize takes your prompt set and suggested quality targets and returns recommended quant profile plus expected % token-cost savings and an estimated quality delta. We show a 'confidence' band derived from similar model runs.
[09:11] Nora: For the pilot we'll probably want: hosted bench to start (fast), then a dedicated small pool in our EU region for production tests. Is that workable?
[09:20] Jordan: Totally. Pilot plan we recommend: 1) hosted bench to validate model picks 2) short dedicated trial (2-4 GPUs reserved) to measure steady-state latency 3) ramp to dedicated commit if economics fit.
[09:33] [09:33] Priya: I'll note down bench parameters: 1k request mix, 70% 512 tokens / 30% 8k tokens, 2M tokens/day extrapolate, target P95 <= 200ms for 512s and aim below 600ms for 8k.
[09:47] Hassan: Sounds reasonable. A couple more nitty-grittys: what telemetry do we need to ship so you can run Optimize and suggest quant profiles? We were thinking of sending samples and CPU/GPU specs.
[09:56] Priya: We'll need anonymized prompt set, tail latency targets, and a small trace for a long-run request. Also hardware details (GPU types, driver/cuda versions). If you're using mixed precision or custom kernels note that.
[10:11] Ethan: For Dedicated private peering, how do we do networking? VPC peering? Direct connect?
[10:16] Jordan: We support VPC peering, private links, and on-prem packages. We'll include the network diagram and the onboarding checklist with IP ranges and peering steps.
[10:27] Amira: Any concerns about egress logs being captured by third parties? We prefer minimal egress.
[10:32] Priya: For Private deployments you control egress. For Hosted we minimize egress and will redact payloads where possible. We can talk about additional data minimization if that's a blocker.
[10:44] [10:44] Jordan: Ok let's recap next steps — we'll send: pricing matrix, bench workbook link (shared), security artifacts and architecture diagram, and propose pilot dates. Also we'll schedule the pilot kickoff. Anything missing?
[10:58] Nora: Could you include estimated engineering effort for a Dedicated pilot? We need an internal resource plan.
[11:02] Jordan: Yes — we'll add an estimated onboarding effort (person-weeks) and an infra checklist.
[11:07] Hassan: One last thing — competitor question: if we evaluate Anthropic or OpenAI, what are the main tradeoffs?
[11:12] Liam: Higher-level: closed models often have better immediate quality but cost more per token and less flexibility for on-prem/private. Open models give you more control and cheaper ops but require more bench and curation work. We'll include an explicit tradeoff table in the follow-up.
[11:27] Amira: Ok thanks — that helps.
[11:30] Jordan: Great. We'll follow up with the artifacts by Friday (2028-03-16). Priya — anything to add?
[11:36] Priya: I'll start the bench harness and share scripts. Also I'll prepare a short demo of the rollback flow for the pilot kickoff.
[11:43] Nora: Perfect. Appreciate the transparency.
[11:46] Jordan: Thanks everyone. We'll send notes and link to the recording. Bye.
[11:50] Meeting ended.

Notes on transcription quality and artifacts: occasional speaker labelling errors; some product names transcribed as "Redwood Optimise" or "Q5_K" vs QLoK naming. Links shared: drive.redwood/demo/catalyst-bench-20280314 (bench workbook), https://redwood.ai/security/soc2 (security packet), pricing: drive.redwood/pricing/catalyst-proposal-03-14 (to be sent).
